clue.text: Get down from there and stop pulling my leg

blocks.note: first meaning: literally climb off something you are standing on
second meaning: an informal retort telling someone to stop teasing or lying

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at a joker perched up high to climb down and quit teasing.
explanation.walkthrough: The same three-word phrase works as a literal order to dismount and as a scoffing reply to nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a literal command to step down from a perch and an idiom of disbelief when someone is joking.

clue.text: Substitute fielder?

blocks.note: first meaning: someone standing in for another
second meaning: a fielding position in cricket, and the player there

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a single cricket substitute, but the two words are separate meanings; cover is an off-side fielding position in cricket, the English bat-and-ball game.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-in worker provides cover, and in cricket the player stationed at that off-side position is also called cover.

clue.text: Crazy set of directions were rational

blocks.note: crazy means mad
six compass points in a row: east, south, east, north, south, east

explanation.surface: Mad-sounding instructions somehow turned out to be sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points supply single letters, and a 'set' of them can be any string of N, S, E and W the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: To make sense is to be logical or coherent, a close match for being reasonable.

clue.text: Demolish old book, well read

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
B is the abbreviation for book
someone well read is literate

explanation.surface: An instruction to destroy an old volume that has been thoroughly read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well read' seems to describe the book, but it is a separate piece meaning educated.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean destroy completely, wiping something out so nothing remains standing.

clue.text: Evasive talk from the cloth

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for waffle meant to dodge a question
second meaning: a soft woollen fabric, or a washcloth

explanation.surface: A clergyman, 'the cloth', giving slippery answers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' suggests the clergy, but here it is just fabric. In British English flannel is also slippery, flattering talk, and a face flannel is a washcloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Flannel is soft woven fabric, and in British slang also empty smooth talk used to avoid giving a straight answer.

clue.text: Tours round church build muscle

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: tours are trips
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Walking tours around a church as a way to get fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Build muscle' reads as one fitness phrase, but 'build' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The triceps is the large muscle at the back of the upper arm that straightens the elbow.

clue.text: Farm animal to lower head in river bend

blocks.note: an ox is a farm animal
to bow is to lower your head

explanation.surface: A cow dipping its head to drink at a bend in the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene of an animal drinking at a river hides a plain charade of two short words.
explanation.definitionFit: An oxbow is a sharp U-shaped loop in a meandering river, sometimes cut off to form a lake.

clue.text: Only women in emirate?

blocks.note: surface reading: a Gulf state populated entirely by women
setter's reading: zero men, the letter for nought followed by a word for a male person

explanation.surface: Imagining a Gulf state where only women live.
explanation.walkthrough: If there are only women, there is nought man; write nought as O and the country appears. The question mark flags the looseness: Oman is strictly a sultanate, not an emirate.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a Gulf state on the Arabian Peninsula, loosely described as an emirate since it is ruled by a sultan.

clue.text: Wait around altar finally for her?

definitions.text: Wait around altar finally for her?

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word it follows, so only its closing letter is kept
to be around something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to bide is to wait
the last letter of altar

explanation.surface: Who is the groom waiting for at the altar? Her.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the person you wait at the altar for is the bride.
explanation.definitionFit: At a wedding the groom waits at the altar for the woman he is marrying to arrive.

clue.text: Dishevelled, after a series of blows

blocks.note: first meaning: untidy, especially of hair
second meaning, playful: what you are when gusts of air have struck you, not punches

explanation.surface: Someone looking battered after a beating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blows' suggests punches, but the blows here are gusts of wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair or clothes messed up by strong gusts look untidy, so being wind-battered and looking scruffy are the same state.

clue.text: Gore beginning to drop into tube

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is taken
going into something means being placed inside it

blocks.note: the first letter of drop
a vial is a small glass tube

explanation.surface: Blood starting to drip into a test tube.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gore' looks like blood but is the first name of the American writer Gore Vidal.
explanation.definitionFit: Gore is the first name of the American novelist and essayist, so the forename defines the surname.

clue.text: Vigour I am contributing to a country

indicators.note: to contribute to something is to put yourself into it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written
a nation is a country
I'm is the contraction of I am

explanation.surface: Someone claiming to bring energy to their country.
explanation.walkthrough: The contraction goes in just after the first letter of the country word.
explanation.definitionFit: Animation means liveliness and energy, as in speaking with great animation.

clue.text: Detect person's elastic slipping, a source of optimistic views

indicators.note: something slipping moves out of place, so the letters shift into a new order

blocks.note: all twenty letters used, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Noticing someone's waistband is sagging.
explanation.walkthrough: A long anagram: the three opening words use every letter exactly once.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking through rose-tinted spectacles means seeing things as better than they are, so they are figuratively a source of an upbeat outlook.

clue.text: Sounds from cat in fashionable street

blocks.note: first meaning: the thin crying noises a cat makes
second meaning: a row of former stables converted into desirable homes

explanation.surface: A cat miaowing in a smart street.
explanation.walkthrough: A mews is a British street of old stables and coach houses, now smart and expensive homes.
explanation.definitionFit: Cats make small crying noises, and in London a converted stable lane is a highly desirable residential address.

clue.text: Swindle over farm machinery one is engaged to supply

blocks.note: a con is a swindle
a tractor is a farm machine

explanation.surface: A fraud involving farm equipment sold by a supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so the first piece sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A contractor is a person or firm hired under an agreement to provide goods or services.

clue.text: Numbers of species left common

blocks.note: genera are the biological groups, each made up of a number of species
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Remaining species populations are widespread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' means groups here: a genus is a group of related species, plural genera.
explanation.definitionFit: Something general is widespread and shared by most, just as something common is.

clue.text: Fruit cooked? It used to be fired

blocks.note: grapes are fruit
cooked food is hot

explanation.surface: Asking whether fruit was baked, as pottery is fired in a kiln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' suggests a kiln or cooking, but it means shot from a cannon.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapeshot was a cluster of small iron balls loaded into old cannons and shot at close range.

clue.text: Grouse distractedly about Conservative whip

indicators.note: a distracted mind is scattered, so the letters are thrown into disorder
about means surrounding, so one piece is placed round another

blocks.note: taken as written
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Complaining in a muddled way about a Tory party whip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip' suggests the parliamentary enforcer, but it is the lash itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourge is a whip used for punishment, and to scourge is to flog.

clue.text: Great duel contested under formal rules

indicators.note: a contested thing is disputed and fought over, so the letters are knocked about

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A famous duel fought by strict etiquette.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an adjective, so 'under formal rules' describes something that is governed by them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something regulated is controlled by official rules, so it operates within a set framework.

clue.text: An improved partner in crime?

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article
improved means better

explanation.surface: An upgraded accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the accomplice's title splits into an article and a comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: An abetter helps or encourages someone committing an offence, as in the legal phrase aiding and abetting.

clue.text: Salesman isn't commonly going to change decor

blocks.note: a rep is a sales representative
ain't is the colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A salesman refusing to redecorate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly' signals the non-standard spoken form of the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To repaint a room is to redecorate it with a fresh coat, altering its look.

clue.text: Not yet in bed, drunk and unable to relax

blocks.note: someone still up has not gone to bed
tight is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Someone still awake, tipsy and wound up.
explanation.walkthrough: Tight is an old informal word for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Uptight describes someone nervously tense and anxious, the opposite of relaxed.

clue.text: Pawnbroker has a name like muck

blocks.note: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A pawnbroker with a dirty reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncle is old British slang for a pawnbroker, as in leaving your watch 'at my uncle's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Muck is dirt, so something resembling it is dirty or impure.

clue.text: The besetting sin of the Greens?

definitions.text: The besetting sin of the Greens?

blocks.note: surface reading: the Green Party and its characteristic failing
setter's reading: people who are green-eyed, the deadly sin that colour is linked with

explanation.surface: A jibe at the chronic weakness of the Green Party.
explanation.walkthrough: Being green with envy links the colour to one of the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Jealousy is traditionally associated with the colour green, the green-eyed monster, and it is one of the seven deadly sins.

clue.text: In Spanish port, a Republican sign

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, here inside the named place

blocks.note: Vigo is a port in north-west Spain
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A political placard in a Spanish harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' looks like a poster but is a sign of the zodiac.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgo, the virgin, is one of the twelve zodiac signs, covering late August to late September.

clue.text: See 11
Part of play understood when listening

indicators.note: listening means taking something in by ear, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: seen in the sense of 'I see', meaning grasped

explanation.surface: A section of a drama that makes sense only when heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I see' means I understand, so understood is seen, which sounds the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is divided into acts and those into scenes, each a continuous section of action.

clue.text: Slacking, paid less — only half

indicators.note: keeping only half of a phrase means the answer is a portion sitting inside it, the central part here

blocks.note: the central four of these eight letters, spanning the gap between the words

explanation.surface: A worker slacking off gets only half pay.
explanation.walkthrough: The kept half is the middle four letters of the eight, spanning the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone slacking is not working, and being inactive or lazy is being unoccupied.

clue.text: Exhausting journey to get computer equipment

blocks.note: first meaning: a tough, tiring trip by car
second meaning: the disk unit that stores a computer's data

explanation.surface: A long trip to buy something for a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase is a gruelling car journey and a storage device.
explanation.definitionFit: A difficult road trip is literally a demanding motoring stint, and the phrase also names a computer's main storage disk.

clue.text: Name of songbird, extremely large

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the two outermost letters of a word

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Naming a songbird that is unusually big.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for large, but it keeps only its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A title is the name given to a book, film or piece of music.

clue.text: Being tense, ramble about buried valuables

blocks.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
to rove is to wander about

explanation.surface: An anxious treasure hunter wandering around a hoard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' seems to mean nervous, but it is the grammar term, abbreviated to one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A trove, as in treasure trove, is a hidden store of valuables found in the ground.

clue.text: Big rodent on the loose in Kentish Town

indicators.note: something on the loose runs about freely, so the letters scatter into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A giant rat escaped in the London district of Kentish Town.
explanation.walkthrough: Kentish Town is a real area of north London, but here it just means a town in Kent, the county south-east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonbridge is a market town in the English county of Kent, so it is literally a Kentish town.
